definition: Morphological antialiasing (MLAA) is a spatial anti-aliasing technique, meaning that it reduces artifacts, such as jaggies, when representing a high-resolution image at a lower resolution.
details: MLAA is a post-process filtering which detects borders in the resulting image and then finds specific patterns in these. The anti-aliasing effect is achieved by blending pixels in these borders, according to the pattern they belong to and their position within the pattern. It is most commonly used in real-time computer graphics. Introduced in 2009, MLAA was an early and influential example of anti-aliasing techniques done in post-processing—applied as a final step to aliased, rendered images—which makes them suitable for deferred shading. A similar method done in post-processing is fast approximate anti-aliasing (FXAA). Another post-process, temporally-amortized supersampling anti-aliasing, commonly known as temporal anti-aliasing, has become the most common anti-aliasing method for real-time rendering and video games. Enhanced subpixel morphological antialiasing (SMAA) is a type of MLAA developed by Universidad de Zaragoza and Crytek in 2011. SMAA improves on traditional MLAA with better pattern recognition (especially for diagonal edges) and local contrast adaptation, which accounts for human perception of edge contrast. explainer.lead: Morphological antialiasing (MLAA) is a spatial anti-aliasing technique that reduces artifacts such as jaggies when a high-resolution image is shown at lower resolution. Introduced in 2009, it was an early and influential post-process approach.

tiers.eli5: After a picture is drawn, the edges look stair-stepped, so you smooth the pixels along those edges.
tiers.practitioner: It runs as a post-process filter: it detects borders in the finished image, finds patterns among them, and blends border pixels according to pattern and position. Being a final step, it cannot fix detail lost earlier in rendering.
tiers.paperLevel: Spatial anti-aliasing via post-process border detection and pattern-based pixel blending in the rendered image; effectiveness depends on how reliably border patterns are detected.

explainer.example: A rendered frame shows jagged edges; MLAA finds the border pixels, classifies their pattern, and blends them to soften the stair-steps.
